569:In the full-information corner case where the router's signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics ($E$ is a deterministic function of $(M,\Sigma)$ and $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ unconditionally; see Part~(iii) of the proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}), $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for the variance contribution of the stripped statistics. The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by KSG~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging $0.075$ nats (Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). Training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); $H(E \mid S)$ alone does not ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$), since routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier (SSR ablation $+43\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}). Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

651:{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone, task and horizon generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone}\label{sec:topk} RR-MoA wins all 21 MOMENT-small/large configurations ($26$--$79\%$; Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}), 18/18 Moirai ($3$--$31\%$), and 6/6 Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} datasets ($37$--$90\%$; Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}): adapter-level and backbone-internal routing operate on complementary axes. The negative controls predicted by Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} (Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, neither using instance normalization) show no collapse and no RR-MoA gain (4/18 within chance; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}). Top-2 sparse routing retains most of the dense gain at a $+10\%$ latency cost (Appendix~\ref{app:topk}); imputation ($7/8$; Appendix~\ref{app:imputation}) and horizons $H{\in}\{96{,}192{,}336{,}720\}$ (24/24; Table~\ref{tab:horizon}) confirm robustness. \textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}) extends to all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table~\ref{tab:residual_ia_plus_mhcb}).}

653	\vspace{-0.6em}
654	\section{Conclusion and Limitations}
655	\vspace{-0.4em}
656	
657	MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs fail for structural reasons: the normalization needed for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs. Raw pre-normalization routing fixes the failure and motivates Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}; $R(\mathcal{D})$ identifies where it applies.
658	
659	\paragraph{Implication.} Routing collapse on instance-normalized backbones illustrates a broader pattern: when a foundation model's input pipeline destroys signal a downstream router needs, optimization-side rescues (load balancing, z-loss, ReLU routing) cannot recover what is structurally absent: the fix is more readily approached by restoring the missing input than by retuning the optimizer. The same mechanism appears in a vision control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); the signal-ratio predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit from raw routing (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, with a held-out boundary case correctly flagged as low-benefit), and generalization to normalization families we did not test is bounded by the assumptions of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.

{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). Two distinct mechanisms contribute. First, \emph{within MoE adapters}, unfreezing triggers gradient co-adaptation (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared backbone, collapsing routing, and freezing prevents this loop and preserves expert diversity. Second, \emph{across architectures}, the frozen five-expert mixture with learned per-sample routing provides an architectural advantage that a single unfrozen head cannot match even with full parameter access: per-sample expert selection captures input-regime structure that no single topology can represent. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. A second architecture introduced below, \textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA), in which each expert has its own sigmoid gate on raw input rather than a shared external router, independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning (learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512, 90 configurations), full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}

{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations; the remaining 5 stay below $0.55$ (vs.\ max ${\approx}1.61$) with high cross-seed variance ($\sigma$ up to $0.71$), indicating stochastic collapse rather than stable partial routing. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps, opposite trajectories from the same code.}

\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility, the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.

366	
367	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
368	\label{sec:rrmoa}
369	
370	An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times h}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states (batch $B$, sequence length $T$, hidden dim $d$) to forecasts of horizon $h$, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. (We use lowercase $h$ for forecast horizon to disambiguate from $\mathbf{H}_\mathrm{FM}$ below, the backbone hidden state.) The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics, so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
371	\begin{equation}
372	\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \widetilde{w}_j \cdot \text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM}),\qquad
373	\widetilde{w}_j = \begin{cases}
374	\dfrac{\exp\!\bigl(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})_j\bigr)}{\sum_{j'\in\mathcal{T}}\exp\!\bigl(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})_{j'}\bigr)}, & j\in\mathcal{T},\\[4pt]

226	\section{Related Work}
227	
228	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; benchmarking work includes TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval}. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies} while keeping a single adapter architecture. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window.

488	In contrast, \textbf{RR-MoA} maintains healthy routing entropy ($1.0$--$1.57$) and wins \textbf{54/54} configurations, with MSE improvements of $26\%$ to $79\%$ over the best fixed adapter. Notably, on Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, where the stripped statistics carry little information), RR-MoA does not improve over fixed adapters, exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}).
489	
490	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep five standard MoE rescue families (Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}) across eleven configurations on 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) actively hurts MSE ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, none of the standard rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate.
491	
492	\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants, all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router, each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual, which closes the DLinear gap.
493	
494	\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$, with no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$ ($15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT), confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) are consistent with the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight controls.

505	C1 & RevIN ablation & Is RevIN the cause? & Entropy $0.000 \to 0.66$--$1.32$ (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}) \\
506	C2 & MOMENT vs Timer-XL & Same code, only norm differs & Opposite trajectories (Fig.~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}) \\
507	C3 & BatchNorm1d / GroupNorm & RevIN-specific or general? & All 3 normalizers collapse identically (App.~\ref{app:norm_generalization}) \\
508	C4 & Rescue sweep (5 families) & Optimization problem? & 0/11 configs recover; $2.7{\times}$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}) \\
509	C5 & AdaMix + raw router & Router architecture or input? & Entropy $\to 1.41$--$1.57$; MSE $-41$--$88\%$ (App.~\ref{app:adamix_details}) \\
510	C6 & SR-MoA raw vs hidden & Generalizes beyond RR-MoA? & Hidden: $+87$--$768\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}) \\
511	C7 & Vision ViT + InstanceNorm & Domain-specific? & Same collapse on CIFAR-10 (App.~\ref{app:vision_moe}) \\
512	C8 & $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection & Just append stats back? & $+42$--$239\%$ worse; 11/18 collapsed (App.~\ref{app:reinjection}) \\
513	\bottomrule
514	\end{tabular}
515	\end{table}
516	
517	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the diagnosis matters more than the architectural label.} The MoE community has framed routing collapse as both an \emph{optimization} problem (load balancing, z-loss all attack training dynamics; effective when router input is informative but under-optimized) and a \emph{post-training representation} problem~\citep{chi2022representation,hua2025inputaware}, where token features cluster around expert centroids. Our setting is upstream of both: an \emph{architectural inductive bias} (RevIN) strips the per-window statistics that carry the routing signal \emph{before training starts}. Optimization-side rescue mechanisms cannot recover what is structurally absent (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and post-training representation fixes presuppose information the input never carried. The mechanism decomposes into two distinct gains: \emph{(Q1)} the best fixed adapter on the same RevIN-normalized hidden states still loses to RR-MoA by $26$--$79\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), so residual shape heterogeneity survives normalization and rewards diverse experts; \emph{(Q2)} the signal-ratio $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ measures \emph{dispatch}-signal localization in the stripped statistics, which is why dense routing also benefits from raw access and why Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) correctly does not improve. The Pure Raw-MLP MoE ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:raw_mlp_moe}) makes this concrete: when the router goes to near-uniform on raw input, the architecture behaves as a raw-input ensemble, sufficient on Weather/ETTm2/Electricity (DLinear regime) but insufficient on ETT-temperature data where the TSFM contributes complementary nonlinear structure. The durable contribution is the diagnosis, not the architectural label --- the choice between ``MoE with raw router'' and ``ensemble with raw input'' is dataset-conditional; we claim only that wherever instance normalization sits between input and router, the routing signal needs to be re-injected from upstream.}
518	\vspace{-0.3em}
519	
520	\begin{table}[h]

523	\label{tab:baselines}
524	\small

491:\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants, all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router, each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual, which closes the DLinear gap.
493:\textbf{The principle is architecture-agnostic (SR-MoA).} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, SR-MoA~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree} replaces the external Conv1d router with a per-expert sigmoid gate $\sigma_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})$, with no external router at all. SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). That a different architecture exceeds RR-MoA while sharing only the raw-input principle confirms it is the \emph{principle}, not the specific router design, that drives the gains. The same SR-MoA architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$ ($15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT), confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. A third architecture-level control, \textbf{AdaMix-Raw} (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}), replaces AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router and recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells. All three router instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) are consistent with the same diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Table~\ref{tab:causal_controls} summarizes all eight controls.
1441:\caption{\textbf{SR-MoA architecture (Self-Routed Mixture of Adapters).} Each of $K{=}5$ experts has its own sigmoid gate $\sigma_k$ reading $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, with no external router. The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph{raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle, not the specific router, drives the gains.}
1442:\label{fig:srmoa_arch}

The frozen TSFM produces $\mathbf{H}$, and each expert's contribution is scaled by its self-gate. SR-MoA shares only the \emph{raw-input} principle with RR-MoA (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): the routing architecture is otherwise entirely different. SR-MoA outperforms RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets, providing architecture-agnostic validation that the principle, not the specific router, drives the gains.}

491:\textbf{Three architectural instantiations of one principle.} The diagnosis says: restore raw-input access wherever normalization destroyed it. The paper proposes three variants, all confirming the same diagnosis from different angles. \emph{(i)}~\textbf{RR-MoA} (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, headline contribution): external Conv1d gate reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ and selects Top-K experts; experts read hidden states $\mathbf{H}$. \emph{(ii)}~\textbf{SR-MoA} (Self-Routed MoA, Figure~\ref{fig:srmoa_arch}, architecture-agnostic validation): no external router, each expert has its own sigmoid gate on $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$. \emph{(iii)}~\textbf{Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}} (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}, Figure~\ref{fig:residual_ia_arch}, diagnosis-actionability proof): each expert combines a shared NLinear raw-input branch with a gated backbone residual, which closes the DLinear gap.

Two issues are creating the mess:
1. **X_raw bus sits EAST of σ (at x=8.00)** → dashed arrows fire LEFTWARD into σ.east, clashing head-to-head with the σ→expert arrows that go RIGHTWARD.
2. **Blue H broadcast arrows are slanted from H-trunk through σ to expert** (yshift +0.18 enters expert top), visually passing through the σ diamond, suggesting H feeds σ (wrong — only X_raw should feed σ).

Fix: flip X_raw bus to the LEFT of σ (rightward taps into σ.west, same direction as σ→expert), and L-shape the H taps so their horizontals run at y+0.40, clearing the σ.top apex.

57	\begin{abstract}
58	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT, Moirai, and Chronos ship with a shared, frozen backbone and a task-specific head. Real series mix heterogeneous regimes — quiet baselines, seasonal excursions, abrupt shape changes — whose shape structure survives instance normalization, and different regimes are best served by different aggregation topologies; a single head must commit to one. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) upgrade replaces the head with a router and a pool of architecturally distinct experts, one selected per input window. We identify and characterize a failure mode of this upgrade on every TSFM that uses instance normalization: once any backbone layer is unfrozen, the router converges to a one-hot assignment, routing entropy collapses to $0.000$, and only one expert ever receives a gradient update. We name this \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}. Its mechanism is direct: RevIN, the instance-normalization layer built into MOMENT and inherited by any TSFM that adopts the same recipe, strips the per-window mean and variance the router needs. A $720$-run sweep across five standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) converges to the same collapsed state, recovering at most $10.9\%$ MSE. This is still $2.7\times$ worse than the causal fix below, because the failure is in the router's input, not its optimization. We formalize the mechanism via a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio statistic, computable before training. The statistic predicts which datasets are vulnerable to collapse (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$) and correctly flags boundary datasets where raw routing should not help. The diagnosis prescribes a one-line \emph{causal fix}: \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA wins $54/54$ dataset/freeze-level cells on the primary backbone ($26$--$79\%$ MSE improvement over the best fixed adapter) and generalizes across four further backbones and an imputation task. Eight causal controls including a vision-modality replication isolate the cause to instance normalization, and the diagnosis predicts a verified \emph{Frozen Paradox}: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. Applying the same raw-signal principle at the expert level (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) closes the remaining gap to per-dataset supervised baselines.
59	\end{abstract}

507	C4 & Rescue sweep (5 families) & Optimization problem? & 0/11 configs recover; $2.7{\times}$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}) \\

516	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the diagnosis matters more than the architectural label.} The MoE community has framed routing collapse as both an \emph{optimization} problem (load balancing, z-loss all attack training dynamics; effective when router input is informative but under-optimized) and a \emph{post-training representation} problem~\citep{chi2022representation,hua2025inputaware}, where token features cluster around expert centroids. Our setting is upstream of both: an \emph{architectural inductive bias} (RevIN) strips the per-window statistics that carry the routing signal \emph{before training starts}. Optimization-side rescue mechanisms cannot recover what is structurally absent (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), and post-training representation fixes presuppose information the input never carried. The mechanism decomposes into two distinct gains: \emph{(Q1)} the best fixed adapter on the same RevIN-normalized hidden states still loses to RR-MoA by $26$--$79\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa}), so residual shape heterogeneity survives normalization and rewards diverse experts; \emph{(Q2)} the signal-ratio $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ measures \emph{dispatch}-signal localization in the stripped statistics, which is why dense routing also benefits from raw access and why Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) correctly does not improve. The Pure Raw-MLP MoE ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:raw_mlp_moe}) makes this concrete: when the router goes to near-uniform on raw input, the architecture behaves as a raw-input ensemble, sufficient on Weather/ETTm2/Electricity (DLinear regime) but insufficient on ETT-temperature data where the TSFM contributes complementary nonlinear structure. The durable contribution is the diagnosis, not the architectural label --- the choice between ``MoE with raw router'' and ``ensemble with raw input'' is dataset-conditional; we claim only that wherever instance normalization sits between input and router, the routing signal needs to be re-injected from upstream.}
